content: Metronidazole topical gel is an anti-infective, antiparasitic, and antiprotozoal agent approved by the FDA for the treatment of inflammatory papules and pustules associated with rosacea. It is applied as a thin film to the affected areas twice daily, in the morning and evening, after cleansing the skin. Patients may use cosmetics after applying the gel. The gel is contraindicated in individuals with a known hypersensitivity to metronidazole, parabens, or other components of the formulation. Contact with the eyes should be avoided, as it may cause tearing. If local irritation occurs, patients should reduce the frequency of application or discontinue use. Caution is advised in patients with a history of blood dyscrasia. Adverse reactions reported with topical use include burning, skin irritation, dryness, transient redness, metallic taste, tingling or numbness of extremities, and nausea. Limited information is available regarding postmarketing experiences. Oral metronidazole has been shown to potentiate the anticoagulant effects of coumarin and warfarin, prolonging prothrombin time. The effect of topical metronidazole on prothrombin time is unknown. Metronidazole crosses the placental barrier and enters fetal circulation rapidly. While no fetotoxicity was observed in animal studies, oral metronidazole has been shown to be carcinogenic in some rodents. Therefore, its use during pregnancy should be limited to cases where it is clearly needed. It is secreted in breast milk after oral administration, and a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. There is no FDA guidance on the use of topical metronidazole in pediatric, geriatric, or immunocompromised patients, nor in those with renal or hepatic impairment. Similarly, no specific guidance exists for use in relation to gender, race, or reproductive potential. Metronidazole has demonstrated carcinogenic activity in chronic oral administration studies in mice and rats but not in hamsters. It has also shown mutagenic activity in several in vitro bacterial assay systems. Chromosomal aberrations have been reported in patients with Crohn’s disease treated with high doses of oral metronidazole for extended periods, though no excess chromosomal aberrations were observed in patients treated for shorter durations. The mechanism of action of metronidazole topical gel in treating rosacea is not fully understood but is thought to involve anti-inflammatory effects. Serum concentrations of metronidazole after topical application are significantly lower than those achieved with oral administration, suggesting minimal systemic absorption under normal usage. The gel is supplied in a 45 g aluminum tube and should be stored at controlled room temperature (68° to 77°F or 20° to 25°C). It is for external use only and should not be used near the eyes. Patients should follow their physician's instructions for use. The interaction between alcohol and topical metronidazole has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol consumption while using this medication.
